knowledge.text: Across the historical temperature edits and the current step-3 addition, once the exact target had already been acquired, performing the explicit heat/cool action on the held target at a closed appliance—without inserting it, opening the door first, or cycling the door—was repeatedly accompanied by far less appliance manipulation and often fewer steps. In current pairs, P4/Q4 (heat tomato then put in fridge) shows the strongest contrast: the Parent moved the tomato into the microwave, closed/reopened/examined it repeatedly, later took it out to heat, and finished in 39 steps, while Q4 heated the held tomato at the closed microwave (Q4:6) and placed it after 8 steps. P5/Q5 similarly had Q5 heat at the closed microwave (Q5:4) and win in 7 steps versus the Parent's open-then-heat 8, and P1/Q1 had Q1 cool the held plate at the closed fridge (Q1:7) and still succeed, though an extra empty-cabinet detour made it 9 steps versus the Parent's 8. Earlier pairs showed the same direction for hot potato and heat tomato in S1_R04 and for hot apple in S1_R03. This supports direct held temperature action as a useful manipulation-saving behavior when the exact target is available, not a guarantee that the Candidate will use fewer total steps in every task.

The temperature-conditioned benefit is bounded by prior exact-target discovery: in the current heat-apple pair P3/Q3 neither execution acquired an apple and both hit the 50-step limit without performing a heat action, so the direct-temperature clause had no opportunity to affect the outcome. Historical S1_R04 heat-plate P2/Q2 had the Parent find the plate on a countertop and succeed in 13 steps while the Candidate never reached that countertop, hit 50, and never heated it; in S1_R04 hot-mug P1/Q1 the exact mug was absent, both hit the limit, and the Candidate's refusal to heat a cup substitute avoided a near-match manipulation but did not produce success. These cases support the limit that direct held temperature action helps only after the exact target has been found and does not itself improve search or prevent step-limit failure.

The current search-step rewrite replaced a family-level single-pass sweep with per-container/per-surface candidates and an instruction to leave an already-open empty or previously matched location immediately and, when the same small set keeps reappearing, continue to new candidates within the step budget. In current paired non-desklamp tasks this accompanied rescues where the exact target lay in an uninspected surface: in put-two-book-in-desk (P6/Q6) the Parent cycled among drawers, shelves, desk and sidetable and hit 50 without checking bed1, while Q6 eventually reached bed1 at Q6:33, took book1, placed it at desk, returned to bed for book2, and won at Q6:40; in put-two-creditcard-in-safe (P7/Q7) the Parent spent 24 steps opening drawer1 through drawer8 before reaching the desk at P7:16, whereas Q7 went to desk at Q7:1 and finished in 9 after two sequential safe placements; and in cool-tomato P2/Q2 Q2 found the countertop2 tomato after a short fridge/countertop1/countertop2 sweep and won in 10, while P2 looped through fridge, cabinets, countertops and toaster to 18. Historical S1_R05 clean-butterknife and clean-soapbar pairs had the same direction: the Candidate reached countertop2/shelf1 and won where the Parent exhausted drawers/cabinets and hit the step limit. This supports that per-container/open-surface expansion can produce rescues when the target is actually present in the newly visited location, though the current Q6 rescue occurred only after extensive earlier revisiting.

The broader per-container/open-surface search language did not reliably stop cycling or guarantee finding the target within the budget. In current heat-apple P3/Q3 neither execution found or acquired an apple; both hit the 50-step limit, with Q3 repeatedly cycling among fridge, countertop1/2, cabinet1-4 and drawer1 rather than reaching any successful target. Q6 reached bed1 only at Q6:33 after repeatedly visiting known-empty drawers, shelves and desk, and Q1's extra inspection of an empty cabinet made it one step slower than P1 despite success (9 vs 8). Historical S1_R05 no-exact-target clean-butterknife and clean-soapbar pairs also hit step limits with cycling, and the cool-apple pair succeeded but required 46 steps versus 38. These observations limit the search edit to an occasional rescue/efficiency direction when a useful uninspected surface is eventually reached; they do not show that it prevents step-limit failure when the exact target is absent, unlocated, or found only late.
